name: PolkaVM
baseline: Wasmtime (cranelift); the same table also lists Wasmtime winch, Wasmer singlepass, Wasm3, Wasmi, wazero, CKB VM and Solana RBPF
workload: Three guest programs (pinky, a cycle-accurate NES emulator running a homebrew game; prime-sieve; minimal) built for PolkaVM's RISC-V RV32EM ISA and for WebAssembly for the other VMs; one-shot time including compilation and initialization, steady-state execution time, and compile time.
claimed_speedup: One-shot (compile + init + run) on pinky: PolkaVM 64-bit recompiler 55.408 ms vs Wasmtime (cranelift) 116.002 ms and Wasmer (singlepass) 137.832 ms (about 2.1x and 2.5x, derived from page data); prime-sieve: 14.390 ms vs Wasmtime cranelift 125.107 ms, Wasmtime winch 54.295 ms, Wasmer singlepass 57.379 ms (about 8.7x, 3.8x, 4.0x, derived from page data); compile time on pinky 167.553 us vs Wasmtime cranelift 62.212 ms (about 370x, derived from page data). Steady-state execution is not faster: pinky 6.422 ms vs Wasmtime cranelift 5.776 ms; prime-sieve 2.104 ms vs 2.161 ms (parity).
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.86.0 (rust-toolchain.toml); benchtool built with cargo --release (profile: lto = true, codegen-units = 1); guests built by guest-programs/build-benchmarks.sh (wasm32-unknown-unknown, RISC-V targets); benchtool Cargo.toml at HEAD pins wasmtime 26.0.1, wasmer 5.0.0, wasmi 0.39.1; replication steps (01-build-benchmarks.sh, 02-run-benchmarks.rb, 03-analyze-benchmarks.rb) listed on the page
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3970X 32-Core, x86_64 Linux; results from commit 190ea5ac, timestamp 2024-11-24
tradeoffs: Guests must be compiled for PolkaVM's own RV32EM RISC-V ISA, not WebAssembly; no floating point or SIMD by design; Rust host API (no C API seen in the workspace); sandboxing and gas metering are built in; the interpreter fallback is far slower (pinky 1.689 s one-shot vs 55.408 ms recompiler); README says the project is unfinished and a heavy work in progress.
caveats: Numbers date from November 2024 (Wasmtime 26, Wasmer 5), long before current Wasmtime releases; first-party suite where the workloads were chosen by the PolkaVM author; the VMs execute different binaries (RISC-V for PolkaVM, Wasm for the rest); the win is in one-shot and compile time, while Wasmtime cranelift is faster or equal in steady-state execution on pinky and prime-sieve; the compile-time gap is likely partly because Wasmtime cranelift optimizes while PolkaVM's recompiler is single-pass (README: guaranteed single-pass O(n) compilation).

name: wasm3
baseline: WAMR fast interpreter (iwasm); Wasmtime Pulley interpreter; WasmEdge interpreter
workload: Interpreter-only comparison on the 17 Wasm cases every runtime runs (xmrsplayer audio, AssemblyScript graphql, audio DSP, MVP kernels), CPU time per call, N=10 per platform, Apple M4 Max E-cores and iPhone XS Max (A12) E-cores.
claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time relative to the fastest runtime (lower is better), M4 Max E-cores: wasm3 1.01, WAMR fast-interp 1.63, Wasmtime Pulley 2.09, WasmEdge interpreter 8.42; A12 E-cores: wasm3 1.04, WAMR 1.38, Pulley 1.68, WasmEdge 9.28. About 1.6x faster than WAMR fast-interp and 2.1x faster than Pulley on the M4 (derived from page data). Page text: 'wasm3 is the fastest interpreter on nearly every case it runs'.
compiler_and_flags: wasm3 v0.9.0 built with -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12 -std=c99 -DNDEBUG -fno-exceptions, Apple clang 21.0.0 (Xcode 27.0), no WASI sources; WAMR cmake Release -O3 FAST_INTERP only (AOT/JIT/FAST_JIT off); Pulley rust nightly-2026-07-05, RUSTFLAGS --cfg=pulley_tail_calls, fat LTO
hardware: Apple M4 Max E-cores (MacBook Pro, macOS 27.0); iPhone XS Max A12 Bionic E-cores (iOS 18.7.10)
tradeoffs: Pure interpreter with no JIT or AOT tier: far slower than compiling runtimes. In the wasmi-benchmarks suite (AMD EPYC 7763, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks-plots/HEAD/data/amd-epyc-7763/lin-scale/geomean-execute.svg) execute geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test is wasm3 16.51x vs Wasmtime Cranelift 1.15x and V8 1.05x. Very cheap startup: same suite startup geomean wasm3 lazy 2.77x vs WAMR fast-interp 56.73x, V8 33.27x, Wasmer Cranelift 1484.15x, Wasmtime Cranelift 1634.19x. Of the Wasm 3.0 features the benchmark tested it supports only tail calls and extended-const. Maintainer states the project is in a minimal maintenance phase.
caveats: Benchmark author built WAMR with 29 carried patches and Pulley from a fork branch with 9 extra commits; all configurations are interpreter-only, so this is not a win over JIT/AOT Wasmtime, Wasmer or V8 (and wasm3 loses to them in the wasmi suite). Only Apple Silicon E-cores measured. wasm3 instantiation of extended-const modules costs 62-122x Pulley's time. wasm3's own docs/Performance.md CoreMark table (wasm3 1627.87 vs wasm-micro-runtime 201.61, 8.1x) is dated 2019-2020 and labelled historical by the project. Independent libsodium 2021-Q1 run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks/HEAD/2021-Q1/README.md): WAMR fast-interp slower than wasm3 on every test, native about 30x faster than wasm3 and about 46x faster than WAMR; I derived about 1.5x wasm3 over WAMR from the per-test logs.

baseline: Wasmtime (Cranelift) and V8 (Node.js)

claimed_speedup: MainLoop 24.541 ms to 98.277 us (249.71x, bytes per op 5,598,185 to 324), CallJS 267.10 ns to 93.56 ns (2.86x), CallNative 191.60 ns to 92.67 ns (2.07x), VmNOP2 1.96x, FuncCall 1.81x, MapDelete 1.48x, CallReflect 1.39x.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26.2; go test benchmarks compared with benchstat-style significance; eligible integer loop traces compile to native code on Windows/amd64 and Linux/amd64, other platforms use a portable typed Go executor
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 PRO 7940HS, Windows/amd64
tradeoffs: API-compatible fork that keeps the upstream package name and swaps the import path; adds adaptive quickening, typed traces with native code for supported numeric loop shapes, cheaper Go/JS boundary calls and an opt-in capability sandbox. Native traces cover only supported integer and float accumulation and counter loops.
caveats: The 249.71x headline is one micro benchmark (MainLoop, a counter-loop shape the trace compiler handles); the other significant rows are 1.4x-2.9x and the remaining 48 benchmarks did not change significantly. The repo's benchjs suite compares the same JS workloads with V8 but its results directory is gitignored, so there is no published V8 comparison; V8 would be far faster on compute. name: Julia
language: Julia (C/C++ runtime on LLVM; embeddable from C/C++ through libjulia)
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1, PyPy 3 (7.3.x), Node.js (V8) and OpenJDK HotSpot, on the same CPU-bound algorithms
workload: Single-threaded CPU-bound programs written with the same algorithm in every language: kostya/benchmarks brainfuck interpreter (bench.b, mandel.b) and naive matrix multiply; plb2 nqueen, matmul (1500x1500), sudoku, bedcov.
claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks (https://github.com/kostya/benchmarks), brainfuck bench.b: Julia 1.564 s vs Lua/luajit 5.686 s, Python/pypy 9.398 s, Node.js 2.954 s (Java 1.191 s is faster than Julia); mandel.b: Julia 30.315 s vs luajit 31.804 s, Node.js 34.692 s, pypy 41.153 s (Java 13.041 s faster); matmul without BLAS: Julia 1.113 s vs Java 3.057 s, Node.js 3.212 s, pypy 3.263 s. Ratios on bench.b: about 3.6x vs LuaJIT and 6.0x vs PyPy; about 2.7x vs OpenJDK on naive matmul (derived from page data). Second source, plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2, Apple M1): Julia 1.10.0 nqueen 3.02 s, matmul 0.76 s, sudoku 2.18 s, bedcov 1.96 s vs luajit 5.31/2.66/4.48/10.52 s, PyPy 7.3.14 6.91/4.89/8.82/6.27 s, Java 3.92/1.14/3.20/3.04 s, Node 3.73/2.88/3.77/2.45 s.
compiler_and_flags: kostya/benchmarks: julia v1.11.6 run as `julia --optimize=3 --check-bounds=no`; Java 24.0.2, Node.js v26.5.0, luajit 2.1.1748495995, pypy 7.3.23 (Python 3.11.15), Docker on Debian; run commands in common/commands.mk. plb2 versions in its README table (Julia 1.10.0, Java 20.0.1, PyPy 7.3.14, LuaJIT 2.1, Node 21.5.0).
hardware: kostya/benchmarks: Intel Xeon E-2324G; plb2: Apple M1 MacBook Pro
tradeoffs: Per-process JIT warmup and large footprint (kostya bench.b base RSS about 244 MB vs 2.5 MB for LuaJIT); package precompilation latency; garbage collected; embedding in C++ goes through the libjulia C API and is heavier than embedding LuaJIT.
caveats: Java beats Julia on kostya's bench.b and mandel.b, and in kostya's other tests Julia loses to the baselines (base64 3.085 s vs Node.js 0.635 s and PyPy 3.534 s; primes 0.680 s vs luajit 0.309 s, Node.js 0.207 s and PyPy 0.617 s; JSON3 0.700 s vs PyPy 0.606 s), so the win is workload specific: numeric loops yes, string and allocation-heavy work no. In plb2 Julia beats all four baselines. The kostya run uses --check-bounds=no (bounds checks removed) and plb2's Julia sources use @inbounds in the hot loops, which other languages' sources do not. Julia matmul 0.12-0.17 s rows use BLAS and are not comparable; only 'no BLAS' is a like-for-like loop. kostya times exclude data loading; whether Julia JIT compile time is inside the timed region was not checked.

name: musql
baseline: SQLite (C, via mattn/go-sqlite3); Turso's Go driver is also compared
workload: Read queries over 100,000 rows on disk-backed files with a warm cache, each checked against C SQLite on 40 bind values before timing, then timed for about 200 ms; musql run with and without its JIT (MUSQL_JIT=0).
claimed_speedup: Apple M4, JIT vs C SQLite: filtered count with one predicate 28 us vs 2.17 ms (77x), two predicates 92x, sum over a filter 8.5x, grouped aggregate 2.1x, ORDER BY v DESC LIMIT 20 2.7x, whole-table count 1.8x. Intel Xeon D-2123IT: 70x, 65x, 7.6x, 2.4x, 2.0x, 1.6x. Slower rows: rowid lookup 1.8x slower on the Xeon (1.0x on M4), secondary-index equality 1.2x/2.9x slower, indexed equi-join 1.3x slower on the Xeon.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27.0 (go.mod); harness compat-harness/bench_columnar_vs_c_test.go (TestBenchColumnarVsC); JIT on vs MUSQL_JIT=0; C SQLite through cgo
hardware: Apple M4 (arm64, macOS) and Intel Xeon D-2123IT (amd64, Linux)
tradeoffs: SQLite-compatible SQL on a new columnar .musq segment format with an append-only delta; import/export tools to and from SQLite files. The JIT covers only supported scan/filter/aggregate query paths; point lookups and joins do not use it. Pure Go driver, but the benchmark harness needs cgo.
caveats: The win comes from columnar storage plus JIT against SQLite's row store; without the JIT musql is much slower than C SQLite on the same scans (for example 9.83 ms vs 2.17 ms for the one-predicate filtered count on M4). Read workloads only; writes, updates and deletes are skipped in the published harness run (BENCH_SKIP). Microsecond-scale rows vary run to run, more on amd64. The headline 75x is an average over two machines of the best rows. Go toolchain build flags are defaults and not otherwise stated.

name: Perry

Perry loses on loop_overhead (97 ms vs Node 53 ms, Bun 41 ms), roughly ties nested_loops (18 ms vs Node 17 ms), and the README shows the 500k-record JSON pipeline at 1,649 ms vs Node 1,010 ms and Bun 647 ms. A second report in the repo quotes image convolution at 268 ms for Perry with Node 4.5x slower.

name: CPython copy-and-patch JIT
baseline: CPython standard interpreter (tail-calling interpreter on AArch64 macOS), built with all optimizations
workload: pyperformance benchmark suite, JIT-enabled build versus the same CPython build without JIT.
claimed_speedup: Python 3.15 What's New: 7-8% geometric mean improvement for the JIT over the standard CPython interpreter on x86-64 Linux; 11-12% over the tail calling interpreter on AArch64 macOS; per-benchmark JIT vs no-JIT ranges from roughly 15% slowdown to over 100% speedup (ignoring the unpack_sequence microbenchmark).

Per the 3.14 notes it is not recommended for production and free-threaded builds do not support it. Machine-code unwinding support added in 3.15.
caveats: Compares the JIT to CPython's own interpreter, not to PyPy, so it does not beat the listed baselines; the claim is small (7-12% geomean) and some benchmarks slow down. Numbers are summarized from the linked doesjitgobrrr.com run (not opened, host not tried) and no CPU model is given. Included as a flagged entry for the copy-and-patch lineage.

name: Cranelift code generator (Bytecode Alliance Wasmtime)
baseline: V8 (TurboFan) for generated-code speed; WAVM (LLVM-based Wasm engine) for compile speed
workload: WebAssembly programs compiled and run through Wasmtime with Cranelift against V8 and the LLVM-based WAVM engine (Figure 22 of a cited paper, per the Cranelift README).
claimed_speedup: Compilation speed approximately an order of magnitude faster than WAVM (LLVM); generated code about 2% slower than V8 (TurboFan) and about 14% slower than WAVM (LLVM).

Cranelift itself is a Rust library; C and C++ programs reach it through the Wasmtime C API (wasmtime.h, wasm.h) or by compiling Wasm to native code, not through a stable Cranelift C API.

The runtime result is a loss to V8 (about 2% slower) and to LLVM (about 14% slower); the win is compile speed against LLVM. Figures date from the paper, not the current release. rustc_codegen_cranelift is already catalogued separately.

name: DIO-JIT
baseline: CPython 3.8 and 3.9 (PyPy is not compared)
workload: Seven small Python programs (brainfuck interpreter, append3, DNA read, fib(15), hypot on strings, selection sort, trans), pure CPython versus the same code under the DIO-JIT decorator; units are not stated on the page.
claimed_speedup: fib(15): 11.63 vs 1.54 on Python 3.8 and 10.41 vs 1.51 on 3.9 (about 7x); trans 24.22 vs 7.79; append3 23.94 vs 10.70; BF 265.74 vs 134.23; selection sort 46.95 vs 33.88; DNA READ shows little gain (16.96 vs 14.82). The README also claims 500x on a partial-evaluation fib example.
tradeoffs: A JIT that runs inside CPython (3.8 and later, relies on LOAD_METHOD) and optimizes by type specialisation rules; users add @jit.jit decorators. The README says it is not production ready and many specialisation rules are still missing. Programs using bytearray and bytes see no gain.
caveats: No hardware, no units, no CPython build details, and no comparison with PyPy, which is the strong baseline for Python JIT speed. Only microbenchmarks, benchmark scripts are linked from the README but were not opened. Last commit 2021-02-18.

name: Eclipse OpenJ9
baseline: HotSpot (AdoptOpenJDK 11.0.7)
workload: DayTrader7 on WebSphere Liberty with DB2 on a second machine: startup time to 'ready to run a smarter planet', RSS footprint after startup and during load, ramp-up and peak throughput.
claimed_speedup: 51 - 55% faster startup, 45 - 57% smaller startup footprint, 33% smaller footprint during application ramp-up, comparable throughput (OpenJ9 with shared class cache and dynamic AOT versus HotSpot).

Benchmark application depends on WebSphere Liberty and DB2, so it is not easy to reproduce, and the harness is not published (tier C). name: Hana Jit (LLVM-backed Python JIT, hanajit)
baseline: Numba 0.66 (and NumPy 2.x)
workload: Numeric kernels compiled through llvmlite: a 5-operation fused NumPy expression, float reductions, polynomial evaluation, dot product, fib(30) recursion and call/dispatch overhead, compared with NumPy and Numba.
claimed_speedup: 3.0x faster than NumPy and 3.7x faster than Numba on a 5-operation fused expression; fib(30) recursion 1.7x vs Numba; call/dispatch overhead about 46 ns (3.6x less than Numba). On plain scalar loops it is about equal to Numba (fp reduction 0.78 ms vs 0.74 ms, poly5 1.04 ms vs 0.96 ms, dot product 0.80 ms vs 0.74 ms); with the evolve() genetic tuner 0.23 ms, 0.22 ms and 0.31 ms against Numba 0.74 ms, 0.96 ms and 0.74 ms.
compiler_and_flags: LLVM via llvmlite; Numba 0.66 and NumPy 2.x as comparison; flags not stated
hardware: single core in a shared CI container (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Alpha Python package (about 3,000 lines) for numeric and array code; unsupported code falls back to the interpreter; also exports standalone x86-64 executables, WebAssembly and GPU kernels; Python-only, not callable from C++.
caveats: The README itself says ratios are the signal and absolute times are noisy (shared CI container, no CPU model); benchmark scripts exist in benchmarks/ (bench_experimental.py, bench_reductions.py, fourway.py) but were not run or read here. Plain scalar loops tie Numba because both use LLVM; the larger wins come from fusion, dispatch overhead and the opt-in evolve() tuner. The baseline is Numba, not PyPy; the README also claims 10-100x over CPython, which is not a named-incumbent comparison.

name: katsu
baseline: Node.js 26.8.1 (V8); Bun 1.4.0 and Deno 2.9.6 are also measured
workload: Cold start of a one-line console.log program (median of 25 runs after 3 discarded, hyperfine-style harness katsu-bench), plus peak RSS and binary size.
claimed_speedup: Cold start: katsu 0.0.5 1.55 ms vs Node 24.63 ms (the page says 15.9x faster), Bun 4.97 ms (3.2x), Deno 12.49 ms; peak RSS 2.44 MiB vs 48.14 MiB for Node; binary 1.7 MiB vs 139.0 MiB for Node. Compute is a loss: the katsu README gives fib(35) at 875 ms vs 53.4 ms on Node (16.4x slower, as of v0.1.6) and the katsu-bench README (https://github.com/tamnd/katsu-bench, also opened) shows fib 20-25x behind Bun.
compiler_and_flags: katsu built with cargo build --release, later runs from the published tarball; runtimes at latest releases of 2026-08-28; flags for the others not stated
hardware: Apple M4 (10 cores, 24 GB), macOS 15.8 (laptop, turbo on, frequency scaling on)
tradeoffs: Pre-alpha JavaScript/TypeScript runtime in Rust that plans a three-tier engine with a copy-and-patch baseline JIT. No module system, event loop, filesystem or standard library beyond console.log at the time of measurement. 12.31% of test262 passing at v0.1.8.
caveats: The author states the lead exists 'because it does less, not because it is better'. The measured binary is an interpreter with an inline cache, not yet a JIT, and compute is 16-25x slower than Node and Bun. Numbers are the project's own, from a laptop with turbo on and are labelled 'indicative' in the spec. Included mainly as a startup and footprint claim against V8-based Node.

name: libriscv
baseline: LuaJIT (JIT mode); README also compares against wasmtime, wasm3 and Luau
workload: Embedded scripting micro-benchmarks run in the sandbox as RISC-V guest code with binary translation, versus the same tasks as LuaJIT scripts: host-to-guest call overhead, syscall cost, integer math loops, sieve of 10M.
claimed_speedup: Binary-translated libriscv vs LuaJIT gist (median): call overhead 2 ns vs 156 ns, syscall (0 args) 10 ns vs 174 ns, integer math 6 ns vs 52 ns, sieve(10M) 80 ms vs 123 ms; fib(40) row shows parity (66 ns median both).
hardware: Gist does not state the CPU; the README names a Ryzen 7950X for its other charts (CoreMark 38223 vs 41382 native, about 92%).
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; same organisation maintains godot-sandbox (487 stars)
tradeoffs: Emulator and sandbox for precompiled RISC-V programs rather than a general JIT for a dynamic language; full binary translation needs a C compiler (GCC or TCC) at run time, or the generated C99 can be embedded ahead of time for platforms that forbid executable memory. Needs a RISC-V toolchain to build guest code.
caveats: Comparison is not like for like: guest code is C/C++ compiled to RISC-V, LuaJIT runs Lua scripts. The numbers come from author-run gists with no CPU or flags on the gist page, and the workloads are hand-picked for game scripting. README claims such as 'routinely faster than other interpreters, JIT-compilers and binary translators', '3 ns call latency' and 'can call the above function 5.25-7.25 times before wasmtime has called it once' are first-party; the fib(40) row is a tie.

name: Luava
baseline: LuaJ 3.0.1 (the widely used Java Lua implementation); PUC Lua and LuaJIT are not benchmarked
workload: Ten Lua tasks (arithmetic loop, recursive fib, table insert/scan, string concat, closures, coroutines, hash table, OOP metatables, string patterns, sieve), paired interleaved runs against LuaJ, order-flipped, median, warm=6, iters=10, with -Dluava.jit.sync=true.
claimed_speedup: LuaJ time over Luava time: coroutines 234.7 ms vs 4549.9 ms (19.39x), recursive fib 243.8 ms vs 2538.6 ms (10.41x), arithmetic loop 33.7 ms vs 285.6 ms (8.47x), string concat 3.03x, table insert/scan 2.83x, hash table 2.68x, sieve 1.84x, string patterns 1.43x, closures 1.21x, OOP metatables 1.21x; all 10 tasks won.
compiler_and_flags: JDK 21+; -Dluava.jit.sync=true (synchronous JIT compilation); other JVM flags not stated
tradeoffs: Pure-Java Lua 5.4 (register bytecode VM with a tiered JIT, sandboxing with instruction limits, Java interop). Requires JDK 21+. MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft.
caveats: First-party numbers with no hardware stated. The baseline LuaJ interprets Lua 5.2 semantics, while Luava implements 5.4, so the tasks are not exactly equivalent. The README says what remains between Luava and PUC Lua (C) is dispatch cost, so it is probably still slower than C Lua and LuaJIT; neither is measured. Synchronous JIT mode is used for the benchmark, which removes background-compile effects. Very small project (52 commits, 2 stars).
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/jit?l=java topic page (luava listed)

name: oxtra
baseline: QEMU 4.1.0 (x86-64 binary translation)
workload: Static x86-64 guest programs (a primes calculator and gzip 1.10.7 compressing floating-point CSV files of 132 kB, 526 kB and 13 MB) translated to RISC-V by oxtra and by QEMU; also instruction counts and memory use.
claimed_speedup: Paper text: oxtra is 'up to twice as fast as QEMU' for small inputs (primes below 10,000: oxtra median 20.68 ms vs QEMU 54.71 ms; 132 kB gzip), 'merely 25% faster' gzipping 526 kB and 20% faster with 13 MB; but for primes below 1 million oxtra is 35% slower than QEMU (3685 ms vs 2720 ms medians).
compiler_and_flags: Guests built with a modified musl-gcc fork (no SSE) and statically linked; host flags not stated
hardware: No real RISC-V hardware: everything ran inside system-mode QEMU running Fedora RISC-V (host CPU not stated); instruction counts given as a hardware-independent proxy
tradeoffs: Executes statically linked x86-64 programs only, no SSE support, needs a custom musl fork instead of glibc; RISC-V host only.
caveats: Student project paper (not peer reviewed, documentation/paper/Paper.pdf in the repo). Timings were taken under QEMU system emulation, which the authors say obscures the results. The README claims oxtra 'consistently beats qemu in our toy examples', but the paper shows a 35% loss on the larger primes workload. Benchmark input files ship with the paper source. Baseline is not one of PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot.
found_via: WebSearch 'dynamic binary translator OR dynarec faster than QEMU benchmark' surfaced oxtra; then README and documentation/paper/Results.tex via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: pg_jitter
baseline: PostgreSQL LLVM JIT (llvmjit); also PostgreSQL's expression interpreter
workload: PostgreSQL 18.1 queries on 1M-row tables (aggregation, joins, wide rows, text, numeric, jsonb), JIT thresholds set to 0, median of 3 timed runs after 2 warmups, parallel workers off.
claimed_speedup: Benchmark page (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter/blob/master/bench/ARM64/0.3.0/BENCHMARKS_v18.md): SUM_int no JIT 44.859 ms, llvmjit 68.090 ms, sljit 42.401 ms, asmjit 42.201 ms, mir 45.620 ms; GroupBy_5agg no JIT 117.367 ms, llvmjit 149.033 ms, sljit 99.530 ms, asmjit 98.079 ms, mir 125.102 ms. README (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter): compile time 'tens to low hundreds of microseconds' (sljit) and 'hundreds of microseconds' (AsmJit) vs LLVM 'tens to hundreds of milliseconds'; average speedup over the interpreter TPC-C 8%, TPC-H 6%, ecommerce 14%, OLAP 42%, CRM ~400%.
compiler_and_flags: PostgreSQL 18.1; build flags for pg_jitter and PostgreSQL not stated on the page.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, 32 GB RAM, Darwin 25.2.0 arm64
tradeoffs: PostgreSQL extension only; beta quality by its own README; jit_above_cost must be lowered from 100000 to about 200-2000; avoid for point lookups; AsmJit backend only on arm64 and x86_64; adds embedded JIT libraries (sljit, AsmJit, MIR) in place of LLVM.
caveats: First-party benchmarks, one machine, ARM64 only (x86_64 results marked TBD); thresholds forced to 0 so LLVM compile cost is paid on every query, which favours the lightweight backends; per-query gains over the interpreter are small (README: sljit 5-25%); CRM benchmark is synthetic and built to show the strongest cases. The baseline is PostgreSQL's LLVM JIT, not one of the category baselines.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'asmjit benchmark code generation speed compared LLVM xbyak sljit JIT assembler performance' surfaced vladich/pg_jitter

The repo README only says the baseline compiler compiles in negligible time 'similar to interpreters' and generates 'better code than LLVM -O0'.

name: PPy (Pretty Python compiler with LLVM JIT and AOT backends)
baseline: PyPy 3.11.15 (warm); also Numba 0.67, Codon 0.19.6, Cython 3.3, mypyc, Nuitka and CPython 3.14.5
workload: Collatz longest-chain search below 300000, kernel wall time, ten fresh processes each.
claimed_speedup: ppy run (LLVM JIT with Python integer semantics, overflow guards) 41.7 +/- 1.8 ms versus PyPy 3.11 52.8 +/- 0.5 ms (about 1.27x faster, derived from page data) and CPython 3.14 1068.8 +/- 5.5 ms; ppy build --unsafe 30.8 ms versus Numba 32.5 ms, gcc -O3 41.9 ms.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 13.3 -O3, clang 22.1 -O3 for the C rows; PPy built with ppy build / ppy run (LLVM); PyPy 3.11.15 and Numba 0.67 warm

name: pqR (a pretty quick implementation of R)
baseline: GNU R (derived from R-2.15.0; the NEWS compares with R-3.4.0)
workload: Assorted R operations named in the release notes, for example paste and paste0 on character vectors and replacing parts of vectors or lists; the README states that the modifications substantially improve the speed of R.
claimed_speedup: NEWS: paste and paste0 are 'about two to six times faster than in R-3.4.0, and are usually faster than the stri_paste function from the stringi package'; replacing part of a vector or list with [ ], [[ ]] and $ is 'often faster', by up to a factor of two or more for scalar index and value.
tradeoffs: Source-compatible modification of R-2.15.0 (with some modules from R-2.15.1 and later), so it lags current R releases and package compatibility; adds some language extensions such as preliminary automatic differentiation. Includes the R packages and Fortran/C sources of the R distribution.
caveats: Claims are release-note statements without a benchmark script, hardware or compiler flags in the files read; the speedup baseline R-3.4.0 dates from 2017, not current GNU R. The project web page pqR-project.org was not opened. Last release 2020-07-23, so a modern GNU R (byte-compiled, 4.x) may have closed some gaps.
found_via: GitHub: radfordneal repository list (pqR, 'a pretty quick version of R'), then raw README and NEWS

name: Pyccel
language: Python (transpiler that emits Fortran or C)
baseline: CPython (interpreted Python; version inferred 3.12 for the dev-branch table, tables also exist for 3.10, 3.11, 3.13 and 3.14)
workload: 13 numeric kernels (Ackermann, Bellman-Ford, Dijkstra, Euler, midpoint explicit/fixed, RK4, four finite-difference solvers, molecular dynamics, splines); execution time in ms, compilation excluded.
claimed_speedup: pyccel-benchmarks dev-branch execution-time table (ms, CPython column vs pyccel_gnu_c column; the Fortran backend is reported too): Ackermann 456.00 vs 1.33 (Fortran 1.28); Bellman Ford 1950.00 vs 3.28; Euler 3900.00 vs 6.94; Midpoint Fixed 40000.00 vs 47.40; RK4 19800.00 vs 57.00; FD Poisson 6140.00 vs 3.78; FD Laplace 729.00 vs 151.00; M-D 8530.00 vs 74.50; Splines 1770.00 vs 13.30. Ratios across the 13 kernels range from 4.8x (FD Laplace) to 1624.3x (FD Poisson), geometric mean about 336x for the GNU C backend (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: pyccel_gnu_c / pyccel_gnu_fortran configurations with -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -mavx -ffast-math (GNU compiler family, version not stated); Intel-compiler variants also reported
stars_or_usage: 398 stars; on PyPI (2.2.3 per the PyPI JSON API); JOSS 2023 paper (Pyccel: a Python-to-X transpiler for scientific high-performance computing) cited in the README
tradeoffs: Restricted, statically typed Python subset; emits readable C or Fortran that is compiled and wrapped as a Python extension; supports NumPy and SciPy calls through generated code.
caveats: Numbers come from the README of the Pyccel developers' benchmark repository (pyccel/pyccel-benchmarks), not from the project's own repo; CPU model, OS, GNU compiler version and Intel compiler version are not stated; the 'dev branch' table is dated 'Mon Aug 3 10:56:24 UTC 2026' and its Python version (3.12) is inferred from the result image file name devel_performance_312_execution.svg. Execution times exclude compilation (the README compile-time table, unit not labelled and presumably seconds, lists 0.33 to 8.31 per kernel across all tools). The CPython column is plain interpreted Python on scalar-loop style numeric kernels adapted from Burkardt and Barba examples (per the README; I did not open the kernel sources), so the large ratios do not transfer to code that already runs in NumPy. First-party benchmark (the Pyccel team's own repository), hence tier C even though the code, flags and Python versions are public. Pyccel is slower than Pythran on Dijkstra, M-D and FD Laplace in the same table. The JOSS paper was not opened (host blocked), so no peer-reviewed numbers are used.
found_via: WebSearch: pythran vs CPython speedup benchmark C++ Python compiler numba pyccel comparison (JOSS paper hit) -> github.com/pyccel/pyccel and pyccel-benchmarks; PyPI JSON API opened

name: Pyston
baseline: CPython 3.8
workload: Web-serving macrobenchmarks (Pyston's python-macrobenchmarks suite).
claimed_speedup: Pyston 'full' (CPython 3.8.12 fork with DynASM JIT): 'roughly 30% faster than CPython on web serving macrobenchmarks'; Pyston 'lite' (JIT extension module): 'roughly 10% faster on macrobenchmarks'.
tradeoffs: Pyston-full is a CPython 3.8.12 fork with a very-low-overhead JIT (DynASM), quickening, attribute caching and build-process improvements (PGO/BOLT); API compatible but not ABI compatible, so C extensions need recompiling; pyston-lite is a pip-installable JIT extension for CPython 3.7 to 3.10 that stays binary compatible.
caveats: First-party claim without hardware, compiler or per-benchmark numbers; the blog with details (blog.pyston.org) was not reachable. The gains are measured against CPython 3.8-3.10, which predates the adaptive specializing interpreter in CPython 3.11+, so the advantage is likely obsolete. The repo page marks the project as no longer maintained; last commit seen in the feed was 2024-08-12. License is the CPython PSF license (the LICENSE file begins with the Python history text).

name: QuickJS (quickjs-ng)
baseline: Node.js (V8)
workload: Process start plus `console.log(1)` for each runtime, measured with the shell `time` builtin (txiki.js issue #301).
claimed_speedup: `./qjs -e "console.log(1)"` 0.005 s total vs `node -e "console.log(1)"` 0.054 s total (about 11x less startup time, derived from page data); txiki.js 0.115 s.
tradeoffs: Small embeddable engine that aims to support the latest ECMAScript specification; a bytecode interpreter without JIT (plb2 classes QuickJS as purely interpreted), used as the engine of runtimes such as txiki.js (the issue's own subject). Embeds from C and C++.
caveats: Startup only: sustained throughput is far worse than V8. In attractivechaos/plb2 (Apple M1) QuickJS 23-12-09 took nqueen 59.04 s and matmul 135.66 s vs Node 21.5.0 at 3.73 s and 2.88 s. The issue page states no software versions, hardware, OS or flags, and it is unclear whether its `qjs` was Bellard's original or the quickjs-ng fork (the entry's repository is the maintained fork).
found_via: WebSearch 'QuickJS vs Node.js V8 startup time benchmark ...' -> txiki.js issue #301 (opened); plb2 README (opened) for the throughput caveat

name: S6 (DeepMind CPython JIT)
baseline: CPython 3.7 interpreter
workload: Three public pyperformance benchmarks (richards, raytrace, unpack_sequence) run with S6's JIT enabled in CPython 3.7.
claimed_speedup: Richards: 7x over the default Python 3.7 interpreter at 100 iterations, 9.5x average on internal dev machines; raytrace 3-4.5x; unpack_sequence worst case 0.2x (a 5x slowdown) or 0.97x in a tweaked variant; README headline 'up to 10x over CPython for pure Python benchmarks'.
hardware: 'internal dev machines' (no CPU model stated)
tradeoffs: Standalone JIT library for CPython 3.7 (strongjit IR lowered to x86 with asmjit); emits x86 machine code via asmjit; calls into C APIs such as NumPy are bottlenecked by C API call time; needs the project's Docker build.
caveats: Archived on 2023-07-05; DeepMind says it stopped work on S6; the README says most testing used internal or private benchmarks and the public numbers are for three benchmarks with minor modifications. Target is CPython 3.7, long out of support. Hardware unspecified. License file is at src/LICENSE (Apache-2.0), not at the repo root. Last commit date was not visible on the repo page (single commit).

name: Shed Skin
language: Python (transpiler) generating C++; runtime library in C++
baseline: CPython 3.14 (headline claim); CPython 3.10.6 and 3.11.0 in the sieve timing
workload: Over 80 non-trivial example programs (more than 25,000 lines) in the examples directory, plus a sieve example with n=100000000 timed against several Python implementations.
claimed_speedup: Typical speedup of 1-100x over CPython 3.14 (average 20x, median 12x) across the examples. Sieve n=100000000: CPython 3.10.6 13.4 s, CPython 3.11.0 11.4 s, Shed Skin 0.9.9 1.9 s (--int32) and 1.8 s (--int32 --nowrap --nobounds), about 6-7x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Shed Skin flags --int32 --nowrap --nobounds for the fastest sieve run; C++ compiler and optimization flags for the 80-program measurement not stated on the page.
license: GPL-3.0 (compiler); MIT/Expat, BSD-3-Clause and BSL-1.0 for the C++ runtime library; examples individually licensed
tradeoffs: Accepts only a restricted, implicitly statically typed Python 3 subset: about 25 stdlib modules, no external libraries, no nested functions or variable argument counts; depends on the Boehm GC; programs often need refactoring; default integers are int64 (use --int32 for narrower).
caveats: First-party numbers with no CPU model or compiler version on the page; the 1-100x range includes programs chosen by the project and individual speedups are only in an image. The sieve table compares different tools at different CPython versions; README shows a separate comparison of Shed Skin and PyPy against CPython 3.10 (git tag performance_comparison) as an image only. Compared with Numba the README notes Numba defaults to int64, so int width affects the comparison.

name: sjsonnet
baseline: google/jsonnet 0.20.0 (C++ reference implementation) and google/go-jsonnet 0.20.0
workload: Evaluating one large production Jsonnet config (staging/runbot-app.jsonnet in the Databricks codebase, about 6.6 MB of output).
claimed_speedup: Sjsonnet 0.4.3 about 0.10 s vs go-jsonnet 0.20.0 about 6.5 s vs google/jsonnet 0.20.0 about 67 s (about 65x vs go-jsonnet and 670x vs google/jsonnet, derived from page data); README dated May 18, 2023.
tradeoffs: JVM implementation of the Jsonnet language (Scala); best when kept as a warm long-lived process; startup cost of a cold JVM applies for one-shot use.
caveats: The measured file is internal to Databricks and not reproducible; the README says Sjsonnet was run as a long-lived daemon to keep the JVM warm while go-jsonnet and google/jsonnet were run as subprocesses (process start included), so the ratio is not like for like. No hardware, JVM version or flags stated; single data point from 2023. The Databricks 2018 blog post 'Writing a Faster Jsonnet Compiler' is referenced but was not opened.

name: Spinel
baseline: CRuby 4.0.4 (MRI interpreter) and CRuby 4.0.4 with --yjit
workload: 28 benchmarks in the repository's benchmark/ directory (mandelbrot, fib, matmul, nqueens, sieve, binary_trees, json_parse, ao_render and others), compiled ahead of time to native executables by Spinel versus the same scripts run by CRuby.
claimed_speedup: 'Geometric mean: ~8.5x faster than Ruby 4.0.4 with --yjit across the 28 benchmarks (~15.2x against the interpreter)'. Examples vs YJIT: mandelbrot 18 ms vs 938 ms (53.6x), matmul 6.1 ms vs 201 ms (32.9x), binary_trees 2.7 ms vs 13 ms (4.7x), json_parse 28 ms vs 133 ms (4.7x), csv_process 95 ms vs 396 ms (4.2x).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 13.3 builds the generated C; CRuby 4.0.4 (revision b89eb1bc) run with --disable-gems, and with --yjit for the JIT column; each cell is the mean of five runs under `perf stat -r 5`.
hardware: '32-core Linux box' (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: An ahead-of-time compiler for a Ruby subset (see the README Supported Ruby Features section), not a drop-in interpreter: it does whole-program type inference, emits C and invokes the system cc. Compiled binaries start in about 0.8 ms.
caveats: First-party numbers with only a core count for hardware. Sub-10 ms cells are dominated by process startup (README says the ratios are lower bounds). The README itself warns the fib row (44.6x vs YJIT) reflects the C compiler folding a pure call tree at build time. The README also notes YJIT is essentially identical to the interpreter on mandelbrot, nqueens, matmul, partial_sums and sieve.
found_via: kostya/LangArena README (opened) lists Spinel as a Ruby contender; github.com/matz/spinel README and benchmark section opened

name: Tengo
baseline: GopherLua (Lua 5.1 VM in Go), go-lua, goja, starlark-go, gpython, Yaegi, otto, Anko; native Lua and Python 2 listed as reference rows
workload: Recursive fib(35) and tail-call fibt(35) executed by each embeddable Go scripting language.
claimed_speedup: fib(35): Tengo 2,315 ms vs go-lua 4,028 ms, GopherLua 4,409 ms, goja 5,194 ms, starlark-go 6,954 ms, gpython 11,324 ms, Yaegi 11,715 ms, otto 48,539 ms, Anko 52,821 ms; fibt(35): Tengo 3 ms vs Yaegi 10 ms.
tradeoffs: Statically-bytecode-compiled dynamic scripting language with its own syntax (not Lua, Python or JavaScript); pure Go, no cgo, sandbox-friendly.
caveats: Single recursive microbenchmark in the project's own README; hardware, Go version and flags are not stated; the code lives in a separate repo (d5/tengobench) that was not opened. The same README table shows native Lua 5.x at 756 ms and native Python 2 at 1,907 ms, both faster than Tengo (2,315 ms), so Tengo beats other Go-hosted interpreters, not the C implementations of CPython or Lua.

name: Wren
baseline: Lua 5.2.3, Python 3.3.4, Ruby 2.0.0p247 (also Python 2.7.5 and LuaJIT 2.0.2 with JIT off)
workload: Four small benchmarks (method call, DeltaBlue, binary trees, recursive Fibonacci); best of 10 runs, interpreter startup excluded.
claimed_speedup: Method call: wren 0.12s vs lua 0.35s, ruby 0.20s, python3 0.78s. DeltaBlue: wren 0.13s vs python3 0.48s. Binary trees: wren 0.22s vs lua 0.52s, python3 0.38s, ruby 0.24s. Recursive Fibonacci: wren 0.20s vs lua 0.28s, ruby 0.22s, python3 0.57s. (LuaJIT with JIT off is faster on binary trees 0.11s and fib 0.10s.)
compiler_and_flags: Not stated.
hardware: MacBook Pro, 2.3 GHz Intel Core i7, 16 GB 1,600 MHz DDR3 (author's laptop)
tradeoffs: Small class-based language (VM under 4,000 lines); NaN-tagged values, fixed object layout, copy-down inheritance; classes cannot be modified at runtime; compiles as C99 or C++98 and later, embeddable through a C API.
caveats: Numbers are from the early 2010s (Lua 5.2.3, Python 3.3.4, Ruby 2.0.0, DDR3 laptop) and have not been refreshed; modern CPython 3.11+ and Lua 5.4 are faster. Only four microbenchmarks; the author states most benchmarks 'aren't worth the pixels they're printed on'. Wren loses to LuaJIT in interpreter-only mode on binary trees and fib. Compiler and flags not stated. The benchmark harness is in the repo (test/benchmark) but was not opened.

name: YJIT (CRuby)
baseline: CRuby (MRI) bytecode interpreter
workload: ruby-bench micro and macro benchmarks (30k_ifelse, 30k_methods, fib, activerecord, liquid-render, optcarrot, railsbench, lee, binarytrees, nbody, fannkuchredux and others), interpreter time over YJIT time after warmup.

name: Janet
baseline: CPython
workload: No benchmark: the README FAQ ('How fast is it?') gives a qualitative comparison only.

README FAQ: programs 'tend to be a bit faster than they would be in a language like Python' because slow object-oriented abstraction and late-binding lookups are discouraged, while the VM is 'about the same speed as most interpreted languages without a JIT compiler'; it ends with 'YMMV'.
